title: Hearing jazz in New Orleans; making up songs on the levee
summary: She knew Armstrong, Celestin and Bunk Johnson, who also went to church; as kids she and friends made up songs on the levee.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Well, then you have done some church singing indeed. Now tell me, when you grew up, did you only hear the singing in the church? Or did you also hear the blues singing? Did you hear the jazz?

Oh, yes. I couldn't help from hearing it. I knew all about, um, Louis Armstrong and Papa Celestan. I've seen them all my life. And, uh, uh, Kid Kelly and Buck Johnson and all of them. I, uh, I knew all of those people. And, um, I met them. And they used to go to church too. That's why they can play these religious songs. Like, uh, uh, when the saints and, uh, what this other song, uh, we shall walk the streets of glory. And, uh, just a closer walk with these by and by when the morning comes. Because they were brought up in that. There isn't very much different in music. All music is basically the same thing. There isn't but 88 keys on the keyboard. So, you, it is too much different. But the difference in the music is one is reverence to God. And another, well, people might say it's to the devil. But some people just sing, uh, when they're happy, maybe folk songs. You know, they get around the, like down in New Orleans, you know, in the wintertime, we used to be on the levee. The correct word, I think, is used, dike. But we used to get on the levee. That's the high amount of ground that, uh, divides, uh, to protect you from the Mississippi River. You know? We used to, we used to get there. And, uh, we used to sit out there on the levee near the railroad track, the Mississippi River and the levee and the railroad track. And we would just make up songs. They weren't bad songs. We used to, we just made them up to amuse ourselves. We, we weren't rich and we couldn't go to nightclubs, uh, things like that. So we just sat as kids and made up songs and sang by the far. Uh, and, uh, used to eat popcorns and sugar cans and things like that. Had a glorious time. Now tell me, are you still making up songs? Yes. Yeah. I, I, uh, write most of my own songs. That's what I understand. That's what I ask. And can't read a lick of music. No? No. Don't know how to, uh, I don't know how to sight read. I never had a day's lesson in my life. But, uh, I, uh, I hear music. I can hear it. And as I hear it, I sing it that way. And folk thinks it's all right.

Well, I can see that on you when you are singing. You have a kind of, you close your eyes and you sort of listen into yourself. And you can, uh, the one who sees it can well understand that you are listening to what you are going to sing. Now, it must be rather difficult though, to, uh, make music, and also to arrange music, as I see you do, when you don't, can't write. How can you go about it?
